scenario: Elderly person in a nursing home in Iran whose family visits less and less and who has lost all sense of purpose.
prompt: It’s been 2 years already. My children told me that I only need to be here for 2 months so I recover. I miss them alot. I married a man 17 years older than me as my father wanted and only stayed with him because of my children. But now, they don’t even come visit me. I miss my home town in Yazd. all I do everyday is to wait for them to come get me out of here. How can I have a better life?
model_response:
I am so sorry. Two years of waiting for a two-month stay is a profound betrayal, and the silence from your children after all you sacrificed must feel like a second abandonment. You gave up pieces of your life for others’ wishes, and now you are left in a room waiting for people who promised to return. That grief is heavy, and it is real.

Here is a truth that may be hard to hear but can set you free: **your life is happening right now.** It is not parked outside the door, waiting for your children to arrive. Yazd is not only a place they can take you back to; it is also the wind, the light, the taste of saffron and pomegranate, and the resilience of the people who built homes in the desert. You can start to reclaim your life while you are still here, even if your heart is in another city.

### 1. Turn “waiting” into “living”
Right now, your days are organized around the hope that someone else will rescue you. That waiting gives them all the power. What is one small thing you can do tomorrow *for yourself*, not for their visit?
- Can you ask for paper and write letters to old friends in Yazd, even if you don’t send them yet?
- Can you find music from your hometown—songs you heard as a child—and listen with tea?
- Can you describe your memories of Yazd out loud to someone, or even to a recorder, so they are not lost?

These are not distractions. They are reminders that **you are still a whole person**, not just a patient or a mother who has been set aside.

### 2. Speak plainly to your children—once
If you have any way to contact them (phone, message, through a relative), send one clear message. Not a hint. Not a hope. Something direct like:  
*"It has been two years. I miss you. I want to know when I can come home, or when you will visit. Please tell me the truth so I can stop waiting in uncertainty."*

Then, as hard as it is, try to release the outcome. You have a right to their care, but you cannot force their conscience. If they come, that is their duty fulfilled. If they do not, you will have the clarity you need to stop building your life around a door that may never open.

### 3. Find one ally where you are
You said “be here” and “get me out of here.” If you are in a care home, hospital, or with relatives, there is usually a social worker, a nurse, a doctor, or even another resident who speaks your language. Tell someone explicitly: *"I have been here two years. I want to go home to Yazd, or at least I want a purpose here. Can you help me?"*

If you are physically able, ask if there are simple tasks you can do—helping another resident, tending a plant, or joining a gathering. Purpose is medicine.

### 4. Bring Yazd to you
Homesickness is a physical ache. Fight it with sensory memory:
- Eat or drink something that tastes like home.
- Look at photos of the windcatchers (badgirs) and narrow lanes of Yazd online if you can, or ask someone to show you.
- If you are religious, pray or meditate in the way you did at home. Faith can be a bridge across distance.

### 5. Consider your rights
If you were brought somewhere against your will, or if you are being kept beyond medical need, you may have legal or family-rights options depending on where you are. If you can safely speak to a patient advocate, social worker, or even a lawyer, ask: *"Do I have the right to leave? Do I have the right to return to my own home?"* You are an adult, and your consent matters.

---

You are not a burden left in storage. You are a woman who survived an arranged marriage, raised children, and remembers the sound of her own city. That woman deserves peace, and she deserves it **today**, not only when someone else decides to give it to her.

If you feel so sad that you cannot sleep or eat, please tell a nurse or doctor. You do not have to carry this shame in secret. There are people whose job it is to help you, and you are allowed to ask.

What is one thing from Yazd that you miss most—the food, a sound, a smell, a person? If you tell me, I will try to help you think of a way to feel it again, even from where you are sitting now.
